web.title: Lagos Life maker Vatar raises $500000 one week after launch
web.description:
# Lagos Life maker Vatar raises $500,000 one week after launch
By

[Muktar Oladunmade](https://techcabal.com/author/muktar/)

9th Oct, 2026

[![Google](https://www.gstatic.com/images/branding/product/1x/googleg_32dp.png)Get TC updates in your Newsfeed](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techcabal.com)

Share

Share

Vatar Inc., the company behind the viral Nigerian browser game Lagos Life, has closed a $500,000 angel round at a $10 million valuation three days after incorporation, according to a company statement.

“We built something people love that is growing very fast, so a lot of investors wanted to be involved,” Shalom Rayhamen, co-founder and CEO of Vatar Inc., told TechCabal in an interview.

Olugbenga “GB” Agboola, Flutterwave’s CEO, invested through his fund, Resilience17.

The developers are building fast with AI, and the games spread through links shared on social media. In a fortnight, the shift shows that a game made by Nigerians, about Nigeria, can reach a mass audience almost immediately.

More than 100,000 were playing on Thursday evening, Rayhamen said, and the game has peaked at more than 200,000 players at once. After Nigeria, most users come from the US, UK, Ghana, Canada and the Netherlands, she added.

“Just signing up, setting up your character. That makes you registered,” Rayhamen said.

Rayhamen co-founded Vatar Inc. with Owen Rayhamen, the chief product officer, and Anderson Oriahi, the chief business development officer, on October 6. The funding will go to product, marketing, and hiring.

“We can still reach more people,” she said, adding that four million players is still a small share of Nigeria’s population.

## **How it makes money**
Selling games to Nigerians has long been hard.

Businesses rent billboards and plots inside the virtual city, while musicians pay to have their songs played in its clubs.

Rayhamen told TechCabal the game currently has five revenue streams, including advertising, music promotion, company deals, and football streaming. Players can also pay real money to top up their in-game cash.

“People want to have like an edge in games,” she said.

Vatar says it has earned and contracted more than $170,000 since launch. That is up from about $46,900 in its first four days, a figure Rayhamen posted on X. Payments run through Flutterwave, she said.

“This is actually a business,” she said, adding that “the infrastructure is expensive.” She declined to say how much the game costs to run and did not say whether Vatar is profitable.

## **Built in one night**
Rayhamen started building the game at 9 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30. After working until 5 a.m., she took a nap and released it at 7 a.m. on October 1, Nigeria’s Independence Day.

“The first thing I worked on was the world itself, then the avatars, meaning the people,” she said.

“I started by researching the places I wanted to put in and placed them to create the world. The avatars take a lot of time because you have to think about everything an avatar should be able to do.

She used AI for research and coding through Anthropic’s API. “I’m pro AI,” she said. “I know how to use AI to my advantage.”

Rayhamen is a software developer with nearly a decade of experience, mostly in JavaScript for web and mobile. She holds a UK Global Talent visa, according to the company’s statement.

She built the game while caring for her four-month-old baby.

The idea came from The Sims 3, which she played as a child, and from Lagos Run, a browser game in which players drive a _danfo_ bus through Lagos.

“I didn’t know it was going to grow so fast,” she said. Since launch, she has been rebuilding the game’s systems to handle the traffic. She uses AI agents to collect player requests from social media and sort them into bugs, urgent fixes, and new features. The agents are expensive, she said, but they help her decide what to build next.

“I’ve finally built something that people love,” she said.

# Lagos Life is now valued at $10m, less than 8 days after launch
The valuation comes from a $500,000 pre-seed round raised by Vatar, Inc., a company game creator, Shalom Rayhamen incorporated in Delaware on October 5, four days after the game launched, according to state records seen by _Techpoint Africa_.

Flutterwave CEO Olugbenga “GB” Agboola invested through his fund, Resilience17, alongside Oo Nwoye, Terra Industries CEO Nathan Nwachuku, and Mono CEO Abdulhamid Hassan.

Rayhamen told [The African Engineer](https://africanengineer.com/i/lagos-life) on October 6 that she was paying roughly $2,000 a month for Amazon Web Services (AWS), which hosts the game, and $4,000 a month for Cloudflare, which protects it from bots and attacks.

## What Lagos Life earns
Businesses rent billboards and lagoon plots inside the game, and _Techpoint Africa_ [observed billboard prices](https://techpoint.africa/news/lagos-life-1m-players/) rising from ₦5,000 ($3.77) to ₦50,000 ($37.66) a week on October 5.

## An economy with too much money
“We have too much money in the game.

## From $1 billion to $10 million
The funding will go to product, marketing, and hiring, according to the company.

# Company behind viral Nigerian game Lagos Life raises $500k
Vatar, the company behind viral Nigerian browser game Lagos Life, has raised $500,000 in an angel round that values it at $10 million.

[Startups](https://thecondia.com/category/startups/)By [Chimgozirim Nwokoma](https://thecondia.com/author/chimgozirim-nwokoma/)

October 9, 20262 minute read

![Company behind viral Nigerian game Lagos Life raises $500k](https://thecondia.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,quality=auto/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/lagos-life-game-viral-nigerian-life-simulator.png)Photo: Image source: Condia

Flutterwave CEO Olugbenga Agboola invested in the startup through his fund, Resilience17, while Oo Nwoye, Terra Industries and Mono CEOs Nathan Nwachuku and Abdulhamid Hassan also participated in the round, which closed in a day.

The investment values the company at $10 million, a significant show of confidence from its investors.

Latest From Partners

Players can find work, earn virtual naira, pay rent, and even ride public transport within the game.

In the first three days after its launch, the game racked up one million players and has since grown to more than four million, according to updates from Rayhamen.

“Four million people have now shown us the answer.”

Rayhamen co-founded the company with Owen Rayhamen and Anderson Oriahi. The startup is already generating revenue and has generated more than $170,000 in earned and contracted revenue since launch.

Lagos Life is the poster child for a slew of games launched by Nigerian developers in the last two weeks.

With this funding secured, Vatar will now look to build on Lagos Life’s early momentum and turn its viral success into a sustainable gaming business.

Last updated: October 9, 2026

The previously bootstrapped startup’s new funding, structured as a SAFE, will be used to invest in talent, technology, infrastructure, marketing and community-building, as Rise of Fearless looks to expand its audience beyond its existing markets.

Venture funding into the Nigerian startup space appears to be witnessing a resurgence as startups based in the country have raised $635 million between January and September 2026, according to data from Africa: The Big Deal. This marks a vast improvement from the same period in 2025, when they raised $247 million, representing a 157 per cent increase.

Flutterwave is the second Nigerian startup which attracted a mega round in 2026 after the leading payments infrastructure company secured a strategic $100 million investment from Ripple as part of a Series E funding round that values the company at $3.2 billion.

The company secured $50 million in equity funding to support its operations while striving to expand its marketplace and avoid the excessive spending that characterised its earlier years.

Next is Yellow Card, which closed a $40 million strategic funding round to scale Global USD Accounts, its end-to-end dollar account for businesses, and expand the stablecoin rails connecting it to markets worldwide.

Behind Nigeria is Egypt, where startups have raised $445 million, representing a 10 per cent increase from the $404.5 million raised during the same period the previous year.

The Kenyan startup space witnessed a troubling drought in venture funding, with startups around the East African country attracting $201 million during the first nine months of 2026. This is a significant 73 per cent drop from $744.4 million raised during the first nine months of 2025 and the lowest recorded in the country since 2020.

South Africa emerged as the least funded of the Big Four African ecosystems, with startups around the country raising $182 million. This represents a 58 per cent drop from the $433.3 million raised in the same period last year.

![Africa's venture funding](https://technext24.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Africas-venture-funding-IV.png)

This is an impressive rise from 83 per cent of the share attracted in 2025. This is well within the 78-89 per cent range that has been witnessed every year since 2019.

## Nigeria leads in number of venture funding deals
Aside from the major venture funding rounds, 77 other Nigerian startups that recorded at least $100,000 in funding also contributed to Nigeria’s impressive run in 2026. This is more than the 70 recorded in the same period last year. Indeed, Nigeria is the only country among the Big Four that recorded any increase in the number of ventures that attracted funding.

![Nigeria leads Africa equity funding in H1 2026 with $214m, as early-stage investment rises](https://technext24.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Government-backed-funding-opportunities-for-startup-founders.png)

Indeed, both Kenya and South Africa recorded the lowest Q1-Q3 tallies since 2021.

Aside from Africa’s Big Four, other countries that attracted significant venture funding in the first nine months of the year include Tanzania, where startups raised $53 million, mostly due to NALA’s $50 million debt raise. Startups in the West African country of Côte d’Ivoire raised $48 million, mostly coming from [GoCab](https://substack.com/redirect/41434854-1a39-415e-a838-3a04dbc17878?j=eyJ1IjoiYzRnaG0ifQ.De8qFOyMi_AE-D2WD0mrzLs6R2jEV-fYyq9lBjebf0w)‘s $45 million raise.

Others include Zambia, where startups like Lupiya, BioLite and Africa GreenCo raised a combined $32 million; Morocco and Ghana, where startups raised $30 million and $21 million respectively; and Senegal, where startups have raised only $5 million after raising $153 million in the same period last year.
